catalog_quote: [Story 1989:100] Central Carrier is on the border between a language characterized by accent and one characterized by tone. 'Accent' or 'stress' is the better term when single words are considered in their surface forms since a word carries one and only one 'accent'. However, when words (or morphemes) are juxtaposed, then ... perturbations occur which are much more characteristic of a tone language. ... First, there is a phonemic stress which is defined in terms of breath force and which is independent of high tone (pitch accent). It is phonemic since within the phonological word, the location of the syllable carrying stress is unpredictable. Phonological words are not in one-to-one correspondence with grammatical words. Certain grammatical words are enclitic; that is, they are phonologically bound to the preceding grammatical word, constituting with it one phonological word. In grammat…
sweep_summary: Two title-hits for Central Carrier, both obtained and read, neither about Carrier word stress. Leer 1976 (ANLA CA965L1976b, 86-page scan fetched sources from ANLA and scanned page by page) is a comparative Athabaskan tonogenesis manuscript; Carrier occurs only as a column in stem-reflex charts and 'stress'/'accent' never occur — silent on the catalog coding. Hargus 2003 (ANLA CA982H2003, typescript of Hargus 2005 in Athabaskan Prosody; already held under babi1235, copied into carr1249) is on Witsuwit'en and Fort Ware Sekani stress; Central Carrier is named once (typescript p. 26 + fn. 18) as a possible test case for tone-stress interaction, with no placement statement — silent. No first-hand Central Carrier stress statement was read in this sweep, so the catalog's deciding source (Story 1989:100, stem-final stress with a culminative pitch accent; classification 'morphological') stands unchanged; the earlier audit's open wishlist (Gessner 2002 ANLC WP2 soft-404; Walker 1979 and Pike 1986 paywalled; Morice 1932 controlled lending) is untouched.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Story 1989 passage is verbatim on the held page image (printed p.100) and in the held scanned of the whole Cook & Rice volume, including the p.101 enclitic examples and the p.102 no-vowel-length statement; the Gessner 2003 supporting review is also held and matches. (2) The classification MORPHOLOGICAL (stress on the stem syllable = final syllable of the grammatical word, enclitics excluded, independent of the culminative H pitch accent) rests on a 1989 specialist phonology article, held in full, which the only modern instrumental study of Carrier prosody (Gessner 2003, held) treats as the most detailed published account and whose stem-final-stress finding it confirms; Morice 1932 and Prunet 1990 (via Gessner) agree. sources.citation: McDonough, Joyce. 1990. Tone and Accent in Carrier. University of Massachusetts Occasional Papers in Linguistics 16(3) [UMOP 14, Papers in Phonology], art. 4, pp. 51-66.
sources.quote: Reanalysis of Pike (1986) Nak'azdli data: 'Carrier is a pitch accent language with a system like Japanese. The syllable is the bearer of accent and every word has a high tone, either by assigning the high tone to the accented syllable or by a default rule which assigns a high tone to the final syllable of a word ... The contrast in Carrier is between accented vs unaccented morphemes.' No statement about breath-force stress or its location (the word 'stress' occurs only in a Beckman 1986 title).

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1976. Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76 (24 pp.) + typescript (30 pp.), first two chapters of a general paper. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA965L1976b (86 scanned pp.). Glottolog ref 167470.
sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. ... In the case of Athabaskan, however, the development of tone depended not only on the vowel nucleus, but on the final consonant of the syllable. If the final consonant was glottalized, the reflex of the tone is opposite of what it is if the final consonant was not glottalized.
sources.locator: typescript p. 2 (PDF p. 3, read as page image); Chart 4 'Reflexes of Proto-Athabaskan Syllable Types' (PDF p. 20) and Chart 5 'Reflexes of Proto-Athabaskan Stem-final Consonants' (PDF pp. 53-54)
sources.note: Comparative-historical paper on Athabaskan tonogenesis (stem vowel nuclei, glottalized stem-final consonants, spirantization). Carrier appears only as a column in the correspondence charts (Chart 4 syllable-type reflexes; Chart 5 stem-final consonant reflexes) and in a marginal note citing Morice. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the 86-page scanned; nothing on where word stress or the pitch accent falls in Carrier.
